text: The man was Johnny Ringo — one of the most feared gunmen in the territory, an outlaw tied to the same feud that exploded at the O.K. Corral. He had a revolver in his right hand and a single bullet wound in his head. His boots were gone. His feet were wrapped in strips torn from his own undershirt. His gun belt was buckled on upside down. And part of his scalp had been cut away.

Those mountains hold more than one unsolved story. They were the homeland of the Chiricahua Apache. They sheltered outlaws, gave their name to a warrior who escaped a prison train, and turned a blind woman into a legend. They were made by a volcano so violent it makes Mount St. Helens look like a firecracker.
But none of it was here by accident. Its raw material arrived in a violent geological instant.
Some of these balanced rocks weigh hundreds of tons and sit on bases that look like they could tip over in a strong wind. They've stood like that for longer than anyone has been here to watch.
But the rocks are only part of what makes these mountains rare. Some of what lives here was only caught on camera about a decade ago.

In the mid-eighteen hundreds, the most powerful leader among the Chiricahua was a man named Cochise, of the [Chokonen](/ʧoʊkˈoʊnən/) band, whose people lived around Apache Pass and the mountains to the west.

What followed spiraled out of control. Cochise returned under a white flag to ask for his people back. Talks failed. Apaches seized hostages of their own. On February eighth, Cochise and hundreds of warriors attacked, and later killed their captives. Days later, on February nineteenth, soldiers hanged Apache captives near the pass — Cochise's brother among them.
Mangas Coloradas was later seized during peace talks and killed in Army custody, and Cochise became the leading figure of Chiricahua resistance.

By the summer of eighteen eighty-six, Geronimo's free band was down to thirty-seven people: eighteen warriors, thirteen women and six children — chased by thousands of soldiers across two countries. In early September eighteen eighty-six, in Skeleton Canyon, just southeast of the Chiricahua Mountains, they surrendered. Months earlier, at another surrender, he had told an Army general: "Once I moved about like the wind. Now I surrender to you, and that is all."

What we know about his life after that comes largely from his own family. He took a young Mescalero woman, Zanagoliche, from her people and made her his wife, and for many years they lived hidden in the mountains, raising children far from any reservation. Settlers blamed him for raids and thefts — some of which, historians now suspect, he never committed.

Around nineteen oh six, [Massai](/mæsˈaɪ/) was killed by a posse in New Mexico. His daughter, Alberta Begay, later shared the family's memories with historian Eve Ball. Her mother always insisted he was no murderer — that he fought only to protect his family.
Stand there at sunset and you can see why anyone would fight to come home. The canyons drop away in every direction, and the valleys below turn gold.

Curly Bill's real ending is its own mystery. In March eighteen eighty-two, Wyatt Earp said he killed him with a shotgun in a gunfight at a spring in the Whetstone Mountains. Tombstone's Nugget offered a thousand dollars for proof he was dead; the Epitaph offered two thousand for proof he was alive. Nobody ever collected. His grave has never been found.

Just to the southeast lay Skeleton Canyon, a smuggling route to Mexico said to be named for the bones left along it. In eighteen seventy-nine and again in eighteen eighty-one, Cowboys ambushed Mexican travelers there. Out of those attacks grew a legend: a treasure of gold and silver supposedly buried somewhere in the canyon. Treasure hunters have searched for more than a century. Arizona Highways magazine called it just another faded and doubtful legend. People still look.

Neil Erickson was a Swedish immigrant who had fought in the Geronimo campaigns as a cavalry sergeant — and who would later become the very first ranger of the Chiricahua National Forest. Emma Peterson, also from Sweden, had worked as a maid for the Army commander at Fort Craig, New Mexico. They met there, married in eighteen eighty-seven, and claimed a homestead in Bonita Canyon. Neil later wrote that Emma had found the place and thought it was the most gorgeous spot she had ever seen.
